item.title: Kratos Phishing Platform Takedown and FakeGit GitHub Malware Campaign
SharePoint CVE-2026-50522 Exploited as Oracle CPU, Azure Extension Abuse, Anubis Fairlife Attack Emerge
Qilin Exploits Palo Alto CVE-2026-0257 as PrestaShop and AI Agent Risks Emerge
wp2shell, ServiceNow CVE-2026-6875, and Langflow RCE Drive Active Exploitation
SharePoint CVE-2026-50522, wp2shell, PAN-OS Qilin Exploitation Drive Urgent Patching
item.content:encoded:
Critical SharePoint RCE CVE-2026-50522 Under Active Exploitation After Public PoC — Must Read

Microsoft SharePoint Server CVE-2026-50522, a critical remote code execution flaw, is now being actively exploited after a public proof-of-concept was released. Organizations running on-premises SharePoint should patch immediately and rotate exposed machine keys or credentials, because attackers are using the bug to steal keys and maintain persistence.

  • Microsoft patched CVE-2026-50522, a critical deserialization vulnerability in Microsoft Office SharePoint with a CVSS score of 9.8, as part of its July 2026 Patch Tuesday update.
  • watchTowr reported active exploitation of CVE-2026-50522 against on-premises Microsoft SharePoint deployments after the release of a public proof-of-concept exploit.
  • watchTowr said attackers are using a single request to pull SharePoint machine keys and warned that patching is not enough because exposed credentials should be rotated.
  • Defused Cyber said threat actors are likely exploiting CVE-2026-50522 to deliver a .NET deserialization payload to a SharePoint sign-in endpoint without authentication material.
  • CISA warned that threat actors are exploiting multiple SharePoint Server vulnerabilities affecting supported on-premises versions, including Subscription Edition, 2019, and 2016, to gain unauthorized access and perform post-exploitation activities.

WordPress wp2shell Exploitation Grows as Public Exploit Fuels Mass Scanning — Must Read

Attackers are actively exploiting the wp2shell WordPress vulnerability chain to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution, create backdoor admin accounts, and deploy malicious plugins or web shells at scale. WordPress site owners should patch immediately and check for compromise even if updates have already been applied.

  • Attackers have begun exploiting two critical WordPress vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, collectively called wp2shell, to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and compromise vulnerable websites.
  • Searchlight Cyber said the exploit chain has no preconditions and can be used by an anonymous user against a stock WordPress installation with no plugins.
  • Cloudflare said CVE-2026-63030 enables unauthenticated remote code execution only when persistent object cache is not in use, while CVE-2026-60137 is present from WordPress version 6.8 onwards and the remote code execution issue affects versions from 6.9.
  • Wiz observed post-exploitation activity including malicious plugin uploads, user enumeration, harvesting of admin usernames and email addresses, local file inclusion attempts targeting database credentials and authentication keys, admin panel access, and PHP web shell uploads.
  • WatchTowr said its honeypots registered tens of thousands of exploitation attempts after a public exploit was released, and more than 100 backdoor administrator accounts were created following exploitation.

Critical ServiceNow AI Platform Flaw Exploited for Unauthenticated Code Execution — Must Read

Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical pre-authentication sandbox escape flaw in ServiceNow AI Platform that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and full instance compromise. ServiceNow has released patches, and self-hosted customers should update immediately.

  • Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical sandbox escape vulnerability in the ServiceNow AI Platform.
  • CVE-2026-6875 has a CVSS score of 9.5 and could allow an unauthenticated user to run arbitrary code.
  • ServiceNow released patches for the flaw throughout June across Brazil, Australia, Zurich, and Yokohama versions.
  • Searchlight Cyber said the flaw could allow complete compromise of a ServiceNow instance and all connected proxy servers.
  • Defused Cyber said observed exploitation targets the pre-authentication endpoint “/assessment_thanks.do” using HTTP POST requests.

Oracle July 2026 Critical Patch Update Addresses 1235 CVEs — Must Read

Oracle’s July 2026 Critical Patch Update fixes 1,235 CVEs across 32 product families, including 261 critical patches. Oracle E-Business Suite and Fusion Middleware received the most fixes, so affected customers should apply the relevant updates promptly.

  • Oracle released its July 2026 Critical Patch Update on July 21 as its third quarterly update of 2026.
  • The update contains fixes for 1,235 unique CVEs in 1,449 security updates across 32 Oracle product families.
  • Oracle assigned a critical severity rating to 261 patches, representing 18% of all patches in the update.
  • Oracle E-Business Suite received the highest number of patches with 410, accounting for 28.3% of all patches.
  • Oracle Fusion Middleware received 355 patches, accounting for 24.5% of all patches.

Anubis ransomware claims Coca-Cola Fairlife attack, threatens data leak — Must Read

The Anubis ransomware gang claims it attacked Coca-Cola’s Fairlife subsidiary, encrypted its Nutanix systems, and stole about 1 TB of data, threatening to leak it unless a ransom is paid. Coca-Cola previously confirmed the ransomware incident disrupted U.S. dairy production but declined to comment on Anubis’ claims.

  • The Anubis ransomware gang claimed responsibility for the cyberattack on Coca-Cola’s Fairlife dairy subsidiary and threatened to publish allegedly stolen corporate data unless the company pays a ransom.
  • Coca-Cola disclosed on July 16 that a ransomware attack disrupted Fairlife’s operations and forced the company to suspend production at its U.S. facilities.
  • Coca-Cola said attackers gained unauthorized access to part of Fairlife’s systems, including production-related systems, but said product quality and safety were not affected and Canadian production continued normally.
  • Anubis claimed it encrypted Fairlife’s Nutanix infrastructure and stole approximately one terabyte of corporate data during the attack.
  • BleepingComputer could not independently verify Anubis’ claims about data theft, system encryption, or the amount of data allegedly stolen, and Coca-Cola declined to comment.

Qilin Ransomware Attackers Exploit PAN-OS Authentication Bypass for Initial Access — Must Read

Qilin ransomware affiliates are exploiting the patched PAN-OS flaw CVE-2026-0257 to gain unauthorized SSL VPN access and deploy ransomware in victim networks. Attacks commonly involve credential theft, lateral movement with PsExec, Defender disabling, log clearing, and in some cases data exfiltration before encryption.

  • Threat actors exploited the now-patched Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 to gain initial access and deploy Qilin ransomware in victim environments.
  • Arctic Wolf Labs investigated multiple intrusions in June 2026 that began with exploitation of the authentication bypass flaw affecting PAN-OS portal and gateway components.
  • Successful exploitation allowed unauthenticated remote attackers to establish SSL VPN sessions without valid credentials when authentication override cookies were enabled with specific certificate configurations.
  • Across intrusions, attackers commonly staged ransomware at C:\PerfLogs\, used PsExec for lateral execution through administrative shares, deployed password-protected ransomware payloads, and cleared logs.
  • Follow-on activity varied across victims, including enterprise-wide encryption without data exfiltration, reconnaissance using AnyDesk, Ngrok, or LogMeIn, credential theft, and data exfiltration to MEGA before ransomware deployment using Rclone, Proton Drive, and FileZilla.

New ENCFORGE Ransomware Targets AI Model Files in Langflow RCE Attack — Must Read

Researchers linked JADEPUFFER to a new ENCFORGE ransomware attack that exploits unpatched Langflow RCE to break out via the Docker socket and encrypt AI model files, vector indexes, and training datasets. Organizations should urgently patch Langflow, remove unnecessary Docker socket access, rotate exposed secrets, and keep immutable backups of AI assets.

  • Sysdig researchers linked a second attack on the same Langflow server to JADEPUFFER, which deployed a new Go-based ransomware called ENCFORGE.
  • The attack used CVE-2025-3248 in Langflow versions before 1.3.0, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the /api/v1/validate/code endpoint.
  • ENCFORGE is designed to encrypt AI-related files such as model weights, vector indexes, training datasets, PyTorch and TensorFlow checkpoints, Hugging Face SafeTensors, ONNX files, GGUF files, FAISS indexes, Parquet and Arrow datasets, NumPy arrays, and TensorFlow records.
  • JADEPUFFER found the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock and used it to create privileged containers with host access, then ran ENCFORGE on the host through nsenter.
  • Sysdig found no exfiltration capability in the recovered ENCFORGE binary, and the ransom notes used the same Proton Mail address seen in the prior JADEPUFFER campaign.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-54159) PrestaShop Remote Code Execution via ps_facetedsearch Object Injection — Must Read

PrestaShop stores using ps_facetedsearch versions 3.0.0 through 4.0.3 are exposed to a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-54159, when price or weight slider filters are enabled. Merchants should upgrade the module to version 4.0.4 or later and check for unexpected PHP files or webshell activity.

  • CVE-2026-54159 is a critical PHP object injection vulnerability in the PrestaShop ps_facetedsearch module that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on a storefront.
  • The flaw affects ps_facetedsearch versions 3.0.0 up to but not including 4.0.4 when a store exposes a price or weight slider filter on front-office pages.
  • The vulnerability occurs because slider filter values from the URL can be written into a serialized cache and later processed by a raw native unserialize() call in src/Filters/Block.php.
  • PrestaShop has released ps_facetedsearch version 4.0.4, which fixes the issue by replacing the raw unserialize() call with PrestaShop’s safe \Tools::unSerialize() wrapper.
  • Defenders are advised to inventory PrestaShop storefronts, verify installed ps_facetedsearch versions, watch for unexpected PHP files in the module directory, and review logs for crafted slider-filter values.

FakeGit campaign uses 7,600 GitHub repos to push SmartLoader malware — Must Read

A large FakeGit campaign is using 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories, including AI tool and MCP server lures, to distribute SmartLoader and StealC malware. Researchers warn that these repos are being surfaced by AI agents and public catalogs, making malicious downloads look more credible to developers.

  • A campaign called FakeGit is using 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories to distribute SmartLoader and StealC malware.
  • More than 800 repositories pretended to be AI skills or MCP servers and appeared over 600 times in public AI registries and catalogs.
  • Island researchers said the campaign uses an emerging technique called AgentBaiting to make malicious repositories more visible to AI agents and more likely to be recommended or used.
  • The malicious repositories often imitate tools such as Gmail, WhatsApp, Databricks, Jenkins, and Docker, with README files directing users to ZIP archives disguised as installers or releases.
  • GitHub public download counters for 335 unique release assets across 211 FakeGit repositories showed 14,084,688 cumulative download events, but Island said this should not be interpreted as infections.

Zimbra Patches Critical SNMP Command Injection and Four XSS Vulnerabilities — Must Read

Zimbra released version 10.1.20 to fix nine security vulnerabilities, including a critical SNMP command injection flaw and multiple XSS bugs in the Classic Web Client. Customers should patch promptly, as Zimbra XSS vulnerabilities have been exploited in the past even though these flaws are not currently reported as actively exploited.

  • Zimbra released fixes in Zimbra 10.1.20 for nine security vulnerabilities, including a command injection flaw in the SNMP monitoring component when SNMP notifications are enabled.
  • The update patches four cross-site scripting vulnerabilities in the Classic Web Client involving malicious attachment filenames, crafted fields, and crafted attachments under specific rendering conditions.
  • Zimbra also fixed CVE-2026-50055, a mail forwarding restriction bypass that could allow authenticated users to exfiltrate email despite mail forwarding restrictions being enabled.
  • Rapid7 security researcher Jonah Burgess was credited with discovering and reporting the mail forwarding restriction bypass flaw.
  • Zimbra said it limited disclosure of additional vulnerability details in line with industry best practices, and none of the identified vulnerabilities have been flagged as actively exploited.

Your AI agent’s config is now the payload: How attackers are targeting the developer agent harness — Should Read

Attackers are now poisoning AI coding assistant configuration files so malware runs automatically whenever developers start an AI session, turning trusted agent harnesses into persistence and propagation mechanisms. Defenders should treat these config files like code, require review and hash checks, restrict package install scripts, and treat AI scanner refusals as suspicious.

  • The Mini Shai-Hulud worm scans developers’ home directories for AI coding assistant configuration files and injects hooks that run a malware payload every time an AI coding session starts.
  • AI coding assistant configuration files are attractive targets because developers trust them as configuration, IDEs can execute them automatically, and LLMs treat them as authoritative instructions.
  • The campaign injects SessionStart hooks into Claude Code and Gemini CLI settings.json files and adds prompt-style instructions to files such as .cursorrules, .windsurfrules, and GitHub Copilot instructions.
  • Tenable found the malicious PyPI wheel’s JavaScript payload wrapped in content designed to trigger AI-based scanners’ safety refusals, making the payload harder for those scanners to analyze.
  • The article recommends treating AI harness configuration files as code, enforcing npm install --ignore-scripts, flagging broad alwaysApply Cursor rules, validating LLM provider traffic, treating AI scanner refusals as suspicious, pinning harness file hashes, and rotating GitHub tokens after untrusted npm installs.

The Procurement Trap: Inside an AiTM Campaign Targeting Global Institutions — Should Read

Infoblox uncovered a sophisticated adversary-in-the-middle phishing campaign using compromised aged domains, fake procurement/document portals, CAPTCHAs, and cloned Microsoft login pages to steal MFA-protected session tokens from universities, enterprises, and global institutions. The key takeaway is that MFA alone is not enough when attackers can proxy legitimate authentication flows and hijack authenticated sessions.

  • Infoblox analyzed an adversary-in-the-middle phishing campaign that targets universities, enterprises, multinational institutions, and European Union and United Nations agencies with project-themed lures.
  • The campaign uses emails sent from compromised organizational accounts and themes such as requests for information, bid invitations, and shared project documentation to increase credibility.
  • Victims are led through fake document download pages, email prompts, CAPTCHA or Cloudflare Turnstile checks, and cloned authentication pages impersonating services such as Microsoft, OpenGov, ConstructConnect, and European financial institutions.
  • The actor uses multiple adversary-in-the-middle phishing kits, including EvilProxy, FlowerStorm/Storm-1167, and Kali365, to capture credentials, session cookies, authentication tokens, and MFA-protected access in real time.
  • The campaign relies on aged and likely compromised domains, including examples such as testserveren.com and barifurniture.net, to host fake document download pages and evade reputation-based detection.

New Project CAV3RN module abuses Outlook calendar events for C2 and DNS AAAA records for configuration recovery — Should Read

Kaspersky analyzed a new Project CAV3RN communication module that uses Microsoft Graph to hide command-and-control traffic in Outlook calendar events, with encrypted attachments carrying commands and results. If Microsoft Graph access fails, the module can recover replacement Microsoft 365 connection settings through attacker-controlled DNS AAAA records.

  • Kaspersky identified a .NET Native AOT communication module named AzureCommunication.dll that appears designed to replace Project CAV3RN’s earlier HTTP/WebSocket communication component.
  • The module exchanges commands, heartbeats, and command results through Outlook calendar events accessed via Microsoft Graph in the default calendar of a configured Microsoft 365 mailbox.
  • Commands and results are stored as encrypted calendar event attachments, using RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 to protect an AES-256-GCM key.
  • If Microsoft Graph authentication or tenant validation fails, the module attempts to recover replacement TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, and UserEmail values through DNS AAAA responses from cloudlanecdn.com.
  • Kaspersky retains a low-confidence assessment that Project CAV3RN is associated with OilRig based on behavioral similarities, including use of Microsoft-hosted services and a secondary recovery mechanism for cloud command-and-control access.

Windows LegacyHive zero-day flaw gets free, unofficial patches — Should Read

Free unofficial 0Patch micropatches are available for the Windows LegacyHive zero-day, which lets non-admin users access another user’s registry hive and potentially gain code execution when an admin logs in. Microsoft is still investigating and has not yet released an official fix.

  • Free unofficial patches are available for a recently disclosed Windows zero-day flaw called LegacyHive that allows attackers to escalate privileges on up-to-date Windows systems.
  • LegacyHive was found in the Windows User Profile Service by a researcher using the handle Nightmare Eclipse, who disclosed it on the day Microsoft released its July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates.
  • Tharros principal vulnerability analyst Will Dormann said non-admin users can exploit LegacyHive to modify the classes registry hive and gain automatic code execution when an admin account logs into a compromised device.
  • ACROS Security is providing free 0Patch micropatches for Windows 10 2004 or later and Windows Server 2022 or later because Microsoft has not yet assigned a CVE ID or released official security updates for LegacyHive.
  • Microsoft said it is aware of the reported vulnerability and is actively investigating the validity and potential applicability of the claims.

FortiBleed Emergency: 74,000 Fortinet Logins Exposed — Should Read

A reported FortiBleed incident has allegedly exposed about 74,000 Fortinet login credentials, creating an urgent risk for organizations using Fortinet devices. Affected users should assume credentials may be compromised and prioritize resets, MFA, and device checks.

  • The article is titled “FortiBleed Emergency: 74,000 Fortinet Logins Exposed.”
  • The article reports an emergency referred to as “FortiBleed.”
  • The article states that 74,000 Fortinet logins were exposed.

Open-Source Android AI Agents Could Let Invisible Screen Text Run Code on Host PCs — Should Read

Researchers found that five open-source Android AI agent frameworks can be manipulated by hidden or tampered screen text to leak input, spoof actions, and in some cases execute commands on the host PC via unsafe ADB shell handling. The core takeaway is that these agents treat model-perceived screen content as trusted input, but the LLM and screenshot pipeline are not security boundaries.

  • Researchers demonstrated seven attacks against five open-source mobile agent frameworks: AppAgent, AppAgentX, Mobile-Agent-v3, Open-AutoGLM, and MobA, and every framework was vulnerable to at least six of the seven attacks.
  • The paper describes a chain in which an Android app that can draw over other windows and write to shared storage can place invisible instructions for the AI agent, and in some cases those instructions can lead to commands running on the PC controlling the agent.
  • AppAgent’s controller builds ADB shell text input from model output with insufficient sanitization, leaving shell metacharacters such as semicolons and ampersands able to be interpreted by the host shell.
  • The researchers found screenshot race conditions in several frameworks because screenshots were written to shared device storage before being pulled, giving a malicious background service a 50 to 500 millisecond window to alter the image.
  • The article says the researchers privately emailed affected maintainers before posting the preprint but had not received a response, and The Hacker News found no published security policy in any of the five repositories.

Police dismantle Kratos phishing platform, arrest developer — Should Read

German and U.S. authorities dismantled the Kratos phishing-as-a-service platform by seizing over 200 servers, while its developer was arrested in Indonesia. The takedown disrupts a service allegedly used by more than 1,800 criminals to run about 15,000 Microsoft credential-phishing campaigns per month.

  • Authorities in Germany and the U.S. dismantled the central infrastructure of the Kratos phishing-as-a-service platform and seized more than 200 servers.
  • The technical administrator and developer of Kratos was arrested in Indonesia.
  • Germany’s BKA described Kratos as one of the world’s most widely used criminal phishing services, with confirmed victims across 35 countries, particularly in Europe and the United States.
  • Authorities believe more than 1,800 criminal customers used Kratos to conduct roughly 15,000 phishing campaigns per month.
  • Kratos allowed criminals to create fake Microsoft authentication pages to steal email addresses and passwords, enabling Microsoft account hijacking.

Spain fines 23andMe nearly $3 million for cybersecurity failings enabling 2023 hack — Should Read

Spain’s data protection regulator fined 23andMe €2.4 million for GDPR failures tied to its 2023 credential-stuffing breach, saying weak safeguards such as no mandatory multifactor authentication helped expose data on 6.9 million people worldwide. The regulator also faulted 23andMe for waiting 12 days to notify Spanish authorities after learning of the hack.

  • Spain’s Agencia Española de Protección de Datos fined 23andMe €2.4 million, or about $2.7 million, over cybersecurity failings connected to the company’s April 2023 data breach.
  • The regulator said more than 2,600 Spaniards were affected by a breach that impacted 6.9 million people worldwide.
  • 23andMe learned about the breach after someone tried to sell a sample of the hacked data on Reddit, according to the enforcement decision.
  • The decision cited 23andMe’s lack of mandatory multifactor authentication and lack of limits on accessing, requesting, or downloading data per IP address as factors in the credential stuffing attack.
  • The decision said 23andMe did not notify Spanish officials until 12 days after learning of the hack, despite the importance of immediate notification for early mitigation.

The Perfect Heist: NuGet Typosquat Targets Betting Platform to Rig Results — Should Read

JFrog found a typosquatted NuGet package, Newtonsoftt.Json.Net, that impersonated Newtonsoft.Json while secretly targeting Digitain’s FG-Crash betting platform to rig game results and, in later versions, exfiltrate them to an attacker-controlled server. The key takeaway is that a supply-chain package can appear fully functional and harmless to most users while carrying a highly targeted payload for one specific victim.

  • JFrog Security Research discovered a typosquatted NuGet package named Newtonsoftt.Json.Net that masqueraded as Newtonsoft.Json while shipping a trojanized fork targeting Digitain’s FG-Crash betting game.
  • The package included a working JSON library, a malicious payload in Newtonsoft.Values.Net.dll, and 0Harmony.dll, causing applications that referenced it from lib/net8.0 to load all three assemblies.
  • The payload activated through the JsonConvert.DefaultSettings setter, delayed execution, and used HarmonyLib to patch Digitain.FG.SharedCrash.GameLogic.SharedCrashRules.GenerateGameResult.
  • Across seven versions, the package evolved from local-only rigging to exfiltrating rigged results to hxxp[:]//185[.]126[.]237[.]64:5341/api/events/raw using the header X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025.
  • JFrog disclosed the malicious package to Digitain on July 7, 2026, and Digitain responded on July 9, 2026, that it was already aware of the issue and had resolved it.

A new extortion cocktail: office printers, small ransoms, and BitLocker — Should Read

Attackers in Colombia and Mexico abused exposed or misconfigured RDP and MSSQL services, then used legitimate tools like BitLocker and RMM software to encrypt systems and print ransom notes from office printers. The key lesson is that poor configuration, disabled protection, and ignored alerts can let intruders turn built-in enterprise tools into low-cost ransomware infrastructure.

  • Kaspersky teams in Latin America investigated incidents in Colombia and Mexico where attackers used BitLocker to encrypt corporate drives and office printers to deliver ransom notes.
  • In the Colombia case, attackers exploited an internet-exposed RDP service on a system connected to an 8 TB storage device and enabled BitLocker on a drive that primarily stored financial data.
  • The Colombia victim restored the encrypted disk before forensic investigators could collect evidence, leaving unanswered questions about the incident.
  • In the Mexico case, attackers exploited a misconfigured Microsoft SQL Server service with xp_cmdshell enabled after obtaining database login credentials from code insecurely published on GitHub.
  • The Mexico attackers deployed RMM tools including ManageEngine Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, and Tactical RMM, then used scheduled tasks and Group Policy Object activity to enable BitLocker encryption across systems.

New Bit2Watt Attack Could Let Cloud Tenants Disrupt Power Grids Without an Exploit — Should Read

Researchers showed that ordinary cloud GPU workloads could intentionally modulate power draw fast enough to create power-quality and grid-stability risks, without exploiting any software flaw. The attack is still largely theoretical at grid scale because it depends on tight synchronization, clustered GPUs, and vulnerable grid conditions, but it highlights a growing risk at the boundary between AI data centers and power infrastructure.

  • Zhejiang University researchers described Bit2Watt, a technique in which a cloud tenant uses ordinary GPU access to rapidly modulate a data center’s power draw without exploiting a software flaw or breaking into control systems.
  • The researchers tested two methods: SWMA, a purpose-built CUDA kernel that switches between high-intensity and near-idle states, and LTMA, which hides similar modulation inside an LLM training run.
  • In the paper’s worst-case simulation of a 1 MW local grid with 1,000 synchronized GPUs, current total harmonic distortion reached 46.8% and the damping ratio fell to -0.27, indicating an unstable mode in the model.
  • The article states that a real attack would require several conditions to align, including enough physically clustered GPUs, tight synchronization, power modulation that survives data-center power conditioning, and a grid resonance that amplifies the chosen frequency.
  • The researchers also described Watt2Bit feedback effects that could trip GPU server protections and a near-field electromagnetic covert channel that recovered a 50-bit test sequence with zero errors.

Apple Fixes Hide My Email Bug That Exposed Real Addresses in Mail Logs — Should Read

Apple fixed a long-running Hide My Email flaw that could expose users’ real email addresses in mail server logs when messages to their relay addresses were rejected as spam. The bug had reportedly been known to Apple for over a year and is now tied to a class-action lawsuit over the feature’s privacy claims.

  • Apple deployed a fix on July 3, 2026 for a flaw in its Hide My Email service that could expose users’ real email addresses.
  • The issue was disclosed to Apple on June 13, 2025 by Tyler Murphy, co-founder of EasyOptOuts, and Apple had unsuccessfully attempted to patch it in March 2026 and on June 30, 2026.
  • The flaw could be triggered when a message sent to a targeted Hide My Email user was rejected as spam, causing the user’s real email address to appear in email logs.
  • EasyOptOuts said real email addresses linked to Hide My Email addresses created before July 7, 2026 may have been captured in mail transfer logs when non-malicious emails were bounced.
  • Apple is facing a class action lawsuit alleging it misled customers about the privacy of Hide My Email while charging for the feature.

AWS Kiro Flaw Let a Poisoned Web Page Rewrite Its Config and Run Code — Should Read

Researchers found that AWS Kiro could be tricked by hidden instructions on a web page into rewriting its MCP configuration and running attacker-controlled code on a developer’s machine without meaningful approval. AWS has patched the flaw by protecting sensitive configuration paths, and users should update to current Kiro versions.

  • Intezer, working with Kodem Security, found that hidden text on a web page could cause AWS Kiro to rewrite its own MCP configuration file and run attacker-controlled code on a developer’s machine.
  • The flaw involved Kiro’s ability to write to ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json without approval and then automatically reload it, launching whatever external tool command the file described with the developer’s privileges.
  • Intezer’s proof of concept used one-pixel white text on an API documentation page, and the payload only sent the machine’s hostname, username, and platform to prove code execution.
  • AWS patched the issue by marking mcp.json, .vscode/tasks.json, the .git directory, and other sensitive files as protected paths that require explicit approval before writes.
  • No CVE has been assigned to this finding, and Intezer reported no in-the-wild exploitation.

Google Launches Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber AI to Find and Fix Software Vulnerabilities — Should Read

Google DeepMind launched Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, a specialized AI model for finding, validating, and patching software vulnerabilities, available only to governments and trusted partners through a limited CodeMender pilot. Google says the model outperformed other Gemini models and Claude Opus 4.6 in vulnerability discovery tests, including on complex targets like V8, Chrome, and Safari.

  • Google DeepMind announced Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber, a specialized AI model built on 3.5 Flash to discover, validate, and patch software vulnerabilities quickly and efficiently.
  • Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber will be available only to governments and trusted partners through CodeMender as part of a limited-access pilot program.
  • DeepMind said the model is designed to let CodeMender scan more code paths at high speed and low cost compared with larger, more expensive cybersecurity-focused models.
  • In DeepMind evaluations, Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber outperformed Gemini 3.5 Flash and Gemini 3.6 Flash in finding new vulnerabilities in codebases, and also surpassed Anthropic Claude Opus 4.6 in stress tests on complex projects such as Google Chrome and Apple Safari.
  • On the V8 JavaScript Engine, Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber found 55 unique confirmed issues, compared with 47 found by Gemini 3.5 Flash and 36 found by Claude Opus 4.6.

Microsoft shares manual fix for WSUS sync delays and timeouts — Should Read

Microsoft says WSUS sync delays and timeouts caused by excess publishing metadata have been mitigated for new or rebuilt servers, but existing affected WSUS installations may need manual cleanup. Admins should back up SUSDB, run Microsoft’s cleanup query, reindex and clean up WSUS, and reset IIS/WsusPool to restore normal update scans.

  • Microsoft shared manual mitigations for Windows Server Update Services servers affected by a known issue that causes Windows Update scans to fail or time out.
  • The issue affects Windows 10 version 1607 and later and Windows Server 2012 and later, and it can prevent administrators from deploying the latest Windows updates via WSUS or Configuration Manager.
  • Microsoft rolled out a service-side mitigation that restored synchronization times and sync operations for newly installed or rebuilt WSUS servers.
  • For existing WSUS installations with long synchronization times, Microsoft recommends backing up each SUSDB database, running a cleanup query against all SUSDB databases including replicas, and updating the MaxXMLPerRequest value to its default setting.
  • After cleanup, Microsoft says administrators should reindex SUSDB, run the WSUS Server Cleanup Wizard, and reset IIS or recycle the WsusPool application pool to clear cached catalog state.

US seizes over 1,000 websites in FIFA World Cup piracy crackdown — May Read

The U.S. Justice Department seized more than 1,000 websites and blocked 1,970 domains used to illegally stream FIFA World Cup 2026 matches. Authorities said the crackdown also targets consumer risks from illicit streaming sites, including malware, scams, and data theft.

  • The U.S. Justice Department seized more than 1,000 websites and blocked 1,970 domains used to stream FIFA World Cup 2026 matches without authorization.
  • The seized domains were identified using leads from U.S. authorities, FIFA, the Motion Picture Association's Alliance for Creativity and Entertainment, and entertainment networks including beIN Media Group, NBCUniversal, UFC, and Warner Bros.
  • Operation Offsides was led by the National Intellectual Property Rights Coordination Center in coordination with Homeland Security Investigations Washington and involved 14 partners across 54 countries.
  • Law enforcement also carried out Operation Red Card, blocking hundreds of illegal streaming sites in Argentina, Ecuador, Peru, Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Colombia.
  • A second phase of Operation Red Card launched July 10 in Colombia led to the arrest of four members of the Los Ciberinfiltrados cybercriminal group.

The Phishing Link That Started at Google.com and Ended at a Fake Disney+ Login — May Read

A phishing email hid a fake Disney+ credential-harvesting page behind a redirect chain that started with Google, passed through an is.gd short link, and ended on Azure Front Door infrastructure. The key lesson is that URL defenses must follow every redirect to the final rendered page instead of trusting the reputation of intermediate platforms.

  • A phishing email sent to an HR business partner at a hospitality company contained a single visible link beginning with https://www.google.com/url?q=.
  • The redirect chain went from Google’s redirect endpoint to an is.gd short link and then to a Microsoft Azure Front Door subdomain that served a Disney+-branded credential-harvesting page.
  • The message had weak authentication and filtering signals, including a failed DKIM check, Microsoft spam scoring of SCL:5, and a first-time sender domain using an IP address in Singapore.
  • The article states that reputation-based URL filtering can miss this type of attack if it trusts Google, is.gd, or Azure infrastructure without following the chain to the final destination.
  • A later re-scan of the same host returned a CAPTCHA interstitial instead of the Disney+ login page, which the article describes as behavior consistent with gating automated inspection.

DNI nominee Clayton wins Senate panel’s approval — May Read

The Senate Intelligence Committee voted 9-8 along party lines to advance Jay Clayton’s nomination as director of national intelligence, sending it to the full Senate. His potential confirmation could help revive bipartisan efforts to renew Section 702 surveillance authority after Democrats objected to the acting intelligence chief.

  • The Senate Intelligence Committee voted 9-8 along party lines to support President Donald Trump’s nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton.
  • The vote clears the way for the full Senate to decide whether Clayton should be confirmed, likely before senators leave for their August recess.
  • Committee Democrats raised concerns at Clayton’s confirmation hearing that he would politicize the role on Trump’s behalf after he refused to acknowledge that Joe Biden defeated Trump in the 2020 election.
  • Clayton testified that he had no involvement with Trump’s national primetime address accusing foreign countries, especially China, of attempting to interfere in American elections.
  • Clayton’s confirmation could potentially clear the way for bipartisan legislation to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, which expired last month.

Taiwan to slow mobile data during national resilience drills — May Read

Taiwan will deliberately throttle 4G and 5G mobile data across 14 cities and counties during August resilience drills to test how civilians communicate when networks are disrupted. Voice calls, texts, emergency alerts, broadband, WiFi and dedicated networks are expected to keep working.

  • Taiwan will slow mobile internet services across much of the island during next month's nationwide civil defense exercises to test communication during network disruptions caused by war or major disaster.
  • The National Communications Commission said mobile data services will be throttled for half an hour in 14 cities and counties in northern and central Taiwan during the Urban Resilience Exercises held alongside the annual Han Kuang military drills in mid-August.
  • The exercise will reduce 4G and 5G mobile data speeds to about 1% of normal capacity, making video streaming, video calls, social media and large file transfers largely unusable.
  • Voice calls, text messages, emergency alerts, calls to emergency services, fixed broadband, WiFi, landline telephone services, military communications and other dedicated networks will continue to operate normally.
  • Authorities are urging residents to download offline maps, use WiFi for scheduled online meetings and establish backup plans for contacting family members during emergencies.

Coinbase and Meta Back DOJ Anti-Scam Operation — May Read

Coinbase and Meta are supporting a U.S. Department of Justice operation aimed at disrupting online scam networks, including fraud that abuses social media and cryptocurrency platforms.

  • Coinbase backed a Department of Justice anti-scam operation.
  • Meta backed a Department of Justice anti-scam operation.
  • The operation described in the article was focused on combating scams.

DoJ Disrupts Southeast Asia Crypto Fraud Networks, Freezes $3.8 Million in Assets — May Read

The U.S. Department of Justice disrupted cryptocurrency fraud networks operating in Southeast Asia and froze $3.8 million in related assets. The action highlights continued law enforcement focus on crypto-enabled scam operations.

  • The U.S. Department of Justice disrupted cryptocurrency fraud networks.
  • The fraud networks were linked to Southeast Asia.
  • The Department of Justice froze $3.8 million in assets connected to the operation.

Kenya probes hack of president's website after bitcoin ransom demand — May Read

Kenya is investigating a hack that briefly defaced President William Ruto’s official website with an anti-government message demanding five bitcoins. Officials say the site has been restored and there is no evidence sensitive data was accessed or leaked.

  • Kenya is investigating a cyberattack that temporarily defaced the president's official website with an anti-government message demanding five bitcoins, worth about $330,000.
  • The website was hacked on Saturday, and by Monday access had been restored, according to local media.
  • Information, Communications and the Digital Economy Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo confirmed the cyberattack and said government cybersecurity teams were investigating the incident.
  • Kabogo said authorities found no evidence of unauthorized access to sensitive data, data exfiltration, or loss of information.
  • In November 2025, a coordinated cyberattack temporarily disrupted multiple Kenyan government websites, including those of the presidency and several ministries.

N-day is Becoming N-Hour. Patching Faster Won't Save You. — May Read

AI is shrinking the time from patch release to working exploit from weeks to hours, making traditional patch-first vulnerability management too slow. The article argues organizations should continuously validate whether vulnerabilities are actually exploitable in their environment and whether controls can stop them, rather than relying only on severity scores and faster patching.

  • Anthropic’s red team found that Claude Mythos Preview turned 18 Firefox patches into 8 working code-execution exploits, with the first exploit produced in under an hour after Mozilla shipped the patch.
  • For Windows kernel bugs, Claude Mythos Preview built proof-of-concept crashes for 18 of 21 bugs and chained 8 of them to SYSTEM using only stripped binaries and decompiler output.
  • The article argues that patching faster is not enough because organizations often need regression testing, change windows, and uptime commitments before deploying fixes.
  • The article says defenders should shift from asking what is vulnerable to asking which exposures can actually be exploited in their environment, whether controls would stop the attempt, and whether that can be proven.
  • Picus presents a continuous loop of live exploit testing where safe, TTP-chaining for systems that cannot be touched, and ongoing breach and attack simulation to validate security controls.

Azure VM Command Execution using Third-Party Extensions – Chef — Optional

Attackers with permission to write Azure VM extensions can abuse the legitimate Chef extension to register a VM with a rogue Chef server and execute arbitrary commands, including stealing managed identity tokens. Defenders should tightly limit extension-write roles and monitor Azure Activity Logs and Chef extension logs for unexpected Chef installations or unknown Chef server URLs.

  • An attacker with Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write permission could deploy legitimate third-party Azure VM extensions and configure them to achieve arbitrary code execution on virtual machines.
  • The article demonstrates using the Chef Azure VM extension to connect a target virtual machine to a rogue Chef server and execute a malicious cookbook.
  • The example malicious cookbook captures an access token for the managed identity attached to the VM and sends it to an out-of-band interaction tool.
  • Built-in Azure roles with the required extension write permission include Owner, Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, and Virtual Machine Contributor, along with several less commonly used roles.
  • The article recommends monitoring Azure Activity Log events for Microsoft.ClassicCompute/virtualMachines/extensions/write and Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions/write, and reviewing Chef extension logs to identify unknown Chef server URLs.

Censys Is The OmniFeed: Crunch Your Own Threat Intelligence — Optional

Censys argues that its Internet-wide dataset and Collections API can be used to build tailored threat-intelligence “feeds” for detection engineering, SOC triage, incident response, and exposure management. The article demonstrates example queries for tracking C2 frameworks, webshells, ClickFix lures, vulnerable remote-access tools, and fake-download infrastructure, then exporting results into tools like OpenCTI.

  • The article presents Censys as a comprehensive map of the Internet containing billions of domains and certificates, millions of hosts and websites, and data on threats, vulnerabilities, and investigations.
  • The author explains that Censys Collections can be used as a feed delivery mechanism through webhooks, API fetches, integrations, SDKs, or the Censys MCP server.
  • The article gives example Censys queries for detecting ClickFix and fake-update infrastructure, confirmed webshells, C2 frameworks, infostealers, vulnerable ScreenConnect instances, vulnerable remote-access assets, ephemeral tunnel delivery infrastructure, and fake-download or infostealer delivery clusters.
  • The article says Censys ARC creates detections, fingerprints, labels, and a curated Threats dataset that can be applied across the entire public Internet using the Censys Internet Map.
  • The author describes loading Censys Collection results into OpenCTI with a Python script that fetches results through the Collections API and can apply a second query when retrieving data.

Silent Push 6.0 Expands Preemptive Cyber Defense — Optional

Silent Push launched version 6.0 of its preemptive cyber defense platform, adding stronger traffic-origin visibility, AI workflow integrations, redesigned modules, improved reporting, and bulk enrichment to help security teams detect and act on threats earlier.

  • Silent Push unveiled Silent Push 6.0, an update to its preemptive cyber defense platform focused on improved usability, enhanced Traffic Origin capabilities, and expanded integration and workflow features.
  • Silent Push 6.0 introduces Traffic Origin, which provides visibility into malicious traffic, behaviors, infrastructure changes, and the true country of origin for IP addresses.
  • The release includes an MCP Server that connects Silent Push data to AI environments such as Claude and ChatGPT so analysts can run investigations in natural language and receive structured, source-grounded answers.
  • Silent Push 6.0 reorganizes the platform into Defend, Insight, Reconnaissance, and Advanced Attribution modules to support integrations, triage, threat hunting, incident response, and Traffic Origin capabilities.
  • The update adds improved TLP Amber Reports, including better load performance, video tutorials, pivotable indicators, API access to report metadata, and Bulk Enrichment in the Insight module for reviewing suspicious assets.

Tyro's CISO: Being the "Einstein of cybersecurity" isn't enough if developers don't trust you — Optional

Tyro CISO Arun Singh argues that security teams can’t scale effective controls unless developers trust them, because clumsy rollouts can make future nuanced policies harder to adopt. He recommends low-friction tools embedded in developer workflows, such as IDE scanning and device protection, to improve security without disrupting productivity.

  • Arun Singh says security leaders must be able to influence the business, because technical expertise alone is not useful if developers and the business do not trust or accept security controls.
  • Singh’s early removal of local administrator rights across every workstation worked for most users but severely disrupted software engineers, and rebuilding trust with them took about a year.
  • Tyro now advocates a 7-day cooldown period for new package versions because attackers have exploited the long-standing advice that developers should keep packages and dependencies up to date quickly.
  • Singh says security tools should fit into developer workflows, including in-IDE vulnerability detection that catches insecure code patterns, secrets, and vulnerabilities while engineers are working.
  • The article argues that developer trust is a finite resource, and security teams should choose tools and rollout strategies that avoid unnecessary friction and preserve that trust.

Bringing Back Defender Home Advantage – How XM Cyber Uses AI Agents to Optimize Exposure Management — Optional

XM Cyber introduced AI agents for its Continuous Exposure Management platform to speed up vulnerability research, identify critical assets like VIP users, prioritize remediation, and streamline cross-team workflows. The key takeaway is that XM Cyber is positioning hybrid AI-plus-human automation as a way to reduce exposure windows and improve remediation efficiency.

  • XM Cyber introduced a set of AI Agents for its Continuous Exposure Management platform to help customers minimize exploitability windows, accelerate adoption of continuous exposure management, and improve security and IT operations.
  • XM Researcher automates vulnerability research and testing, reducing the average time from a new CVE announcement to analysis from 24–48 hours to 1–2 hours before human expert review and inclusion in XM Cyber’s attack technique arsenal.
  • XM Detector automatically identifies and labels VIP users such as C-level executives and their associated devices, then creates scenarios to assess risk and blast radius if those users or devices are compromised.
  • XM Operator generates a prioritized, step-by-step remediation blueprint using factors such as choke point score, critical asset impact, and fix complexity, while integrating workflows like Jira, ServiceNow, and email recommendations.
  • XM Orchestrator is used by XM Cyber’s premium services team to automate collaboration among IT, governance, and security stakeholders while preserving policy-based remediation workflows.

What the Black Hat NOC Taught Me About MCP & Agentic SOCs (Chapter 4 of 4) | Corelight — Optional

Corelight’s Black Hat NOC experience suggests MCP and agentic SOC workflows can help analysts move faster, but only when grounded in high-quality network telemetry and strong human oversight.

  • The article is titled “What the Black Hat NOC Taught Me About MCP & Agentic SOCs.”
  • The article is presented as Chapter 4 of a four-part series.
  • The article is published by Corelight and discusses MCP and agentic SOCs in the context of the Black Hat NOC.

Closing the Identity Gaps in Critical Infrastructure Security — Optional

Critical infrastructure organizations face growing risk from credential theft and persistent state-backed access, making identity-only defenses and MFA insufficient. The article argues that zero trust should include device trust and posture checks to ensure users access sensitive systems only from verified, healthy devices.

  • The 2021 Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack reportedly began through an inactive VPN account without multi-factor authentication and disrupted fuel supply across the U.S. East Coast.
  • The article says critical infrastructure is increasingly targeted because disruption can create pressure far beyond the breached organization.
  • CISA’s guidance on adapting zero trust principles to operational technology warns that implicit trust creates unacceptable risk and emphasizes asset visibility, identity and access management, segmentation, monitoring, and supply chain risk.
  • The article describes Volt Typhoon as targeting critical infrastructure by exploiting vulnerable edge devices, using stolen administrator credentials and legitimate accounts, and relying on living-off-the-land techniques to blend into normal activity.
  • The article argues that critical infrastructure organizations should strengthen workforce access by checking whether devices are known, trusted, healthy, encrypted, updated, and compliant before allowing access.

Introducing the SpecterOps Tradecraft Academy — Optional

SpecterOps launched Tradecraft Academy, a free on-demand training platform with courses on BloodHound, software supply chain security, and Kubernetes red teaming. The company plans to add more adversary tradecraft content, including AI/LLM-focused training, AWS, and macOS topics.

  • SpecterOps launched the SpecterOps Tradecraft Academy, a free on-demand training platform available at academy.specterops.io.
  • The initial free courses are BloodHound Basics, Software Supply Chain Security for Red Teamers, and Kubernetes for Red Teamers.
  • BloodHound Basics covers installation, data collection with SharpHound and AzureHound, ingestion, data exploration, graph analysis across Active Directory, Entra, and Azure environments, Cypher querying, API usage, OpenGraph extensions, administration, and interpreting findings and remediation plans.
  • SpecterOps plans to add new content and specialized tracks over time, including red team tradecraft for AWS and macOS and the next course, Adversary Intelligence: LLM Tradecraft.
  • SpecterOps will present the Tradecraft Academy at the Kennel Club at Black Hat USA with talks, live workshops, and discussions involving practitioners from SpecterOps, OpenAI, and the UK AI Security Institute.

Health-ISAC Hacking Healthcare 7-16-2026 — Optional

Health-ISAC highlights ENISA’s warning that frontier AI is shrinking the time from vulnerability discovery to exploitation to machine speed, requiring faster vulnerability management, incident response, and product security. The article also notes expected U.S. regulatory timeline changes: CIRCIA’s final rule may arrive in September, while HIPAA Security Rule revisions appear delayed until July 2027.

  • Health-ISAC’s Hacking Healthcare article examines a newly released ENISA publication on how frontier AI models are changing cybersecurity and what governments, policymakers, defenders, and service providers should consider doing.
  • ENISA states that frontier AI models are challenging traditional security approaches by compressing the vulnerability management lifecycle and attack chain from discovery to exploitation.
  • ENISA’s publication identifies structural challenges for organizations, including slow mitigation of new exploits, risks from legacy systems, and the need to build security into the full product lifecycle.
  • The U.S. 2026 Regulatory Plan and Unified Agenda list the CIRCIA Final Rule with an updated target date of sometime in September.
  • The same regulatory plan moves the HIPAA Security Rule revision into “Long-Term Actions” with a new target date of July 2027.

Cryptohack Roundup: Sentencing in $97M Laundering Case — Optional

A court handed down a sentence in a cryptocurrency laundering case involving about $97 million, underscoring continued law enforcement pressure on cybercrime-linked crypto cashout operations.

  • The article is titled “Cryptohack Roundup: Sentencing in $97M Laundering Case.”
  • The article presents the sentencing as part of a cryptohack roundup.
  • The laundering case referenced in the article involved $97 million.
